commenti.body:
The most shocking thing about Infinity War is its total amorality.

Thanos's plan is blatantly stupid, yes, but more than that, it is completely unchallenged by the "heroes" of the movie. Our iconic superheroes who are supposed to stand for everything good and right.

Thanos says unchecked life needs "correction". Gamora replies "You don't know that". She doesn't say "killing innocent people is wrong" but effectively, "you can't be sure killing innocent people will lead to your desired result". Wow. What a powerful condemnation, right?

Again, Thanos explains his plan to Doctor Strange and concludes "the hardest choices require the strongest wills". Doctor Strange replies "I think you'll find our will is equal to yours". Not any challenge to his ideology, or his plans, just "we fight now!"

In Endgame, more of the same. Thanos: "The universe required correction." Banner: "You murdered trillions!" I guess that's a little better? Then, without any further meaningful debate, they beat him up and kill him.

No actual refutation of Thanos's evil. No moment when he realizes he was wrong, or his flaws are exposed, or his moral failings lead to his downfall. No symbolic defeat. Just a mindless physical battle, repeated when they fight his alternate self (and the terribleness of that whole plot hardly needs further comment).

There is no moral center here. Especially considering the history of comic books as moral lessons for children, as at least aspiring promoters of social good and change, this absence is stunning.

These movies are paper thin and very superficial but my least favorite thing about them has always been that they feel extremely small and they sell a very poor cinematic illusion, which is the closest thing that big budget studio films have that is “superior” to personal art. I don’t hate the films or anything like that but it’s really hard to feel passionately about them when they only exist to challenge the logistics of actors (which even then they don’t always do authentically). Calling them video games with bad art direction is spot on analysis. 

I actually really strongly disagree with the commonly touted wisdom that Thanos is the protagonist. To me, he is just very much an antagonist that is at the center of the film, but I don’t see him going on a hero’s/antihero’s/antivillain’s journey, I don’t even really see him as being the most dynamic character or the driver of the plot. To me this film is an ensemble the way that all the other superhero team ups are. Fine. 

I do think I prefer Endgame just because I think it has a modicum more of something to actually say, and I think most of the meta moments actually double well as plot beats, Steve’s retirement for example. The fan service isn’t really higher than some others in this one imo, it’s pretty baseline. I think the focus on grief and progress is done as well as you can expect for the kind of movie that it is, whereas I don’t feel like Infinity War is actually about anything. 

To me, divorced from box office and legacy and whatnot, these films feel like the closest analogue to some of those big comedy ensemble films like Mad Mad World. Cool novelty, and amazing to see actors share the screen/story, but not necessarily groundbreaking in their own right.
Man, the similarity to the ensemble comedies of the 60s and 70s is something I hadn't considered but is absolutely spot on!

Yep, the only thing that makes Infinity War somewhat interesting is Thanos being an anti-villain/anti-hero and his amoral philosophy:

His stance is essentially the trolley problem — if you do nothing then many will die, but if you choose to kill some then you can save the others. 

However, like you said, there's barely any further depth added or exploration of that philosophy. 

There's some shallow backstory about how his childhood planet was destroyed due to overpopulation (I'm guessing it's expanded a bit more in the comics), so of course, now he wants to destroy half the population to solve overpopulation all over the universe — genius! 

Why not wish for more resources in every solar system, since you can just magically snap half the population on every planet anyway lmao

As a kid I was a comic book nerd (many, many years ago) and after a while I gave up on the super-hero genre. Mostly this was just aging out of interest in such stories, but another big reason was that it became clear to me at some point that many (if not most) of the creative decisions were being made for the simple goal of separating earnest kids like me from the cash we’d saved up delivering newspapers or whatever. It seemed every other month there was a new *major event* featuring the death of some character, which would inevitably be followed a few months later by a thinly-justified resurrection; or perhaps a long, convoluted saga - similar to Infinity War - which required its readers to scrape together more pocket change to buy issues of series we didn’t normally follow. Slick marketing, but not exactly satisfying on a creative level. 

I was reminded of all this when Endgame came out and I read a number of high-minded reviews that, surprisingly, seemed unaware of the fact that all of those “dead” characters would inevitably be brought back via some cheesy plot gimmick. I’ve only seen a couple of the modern crop of super-hero films, and they were entertaining enough as mindless spectacle. But I have to wonder if the recent explosion of these films & tv series has begun to reach a point for many viewers similar to that I reached as a kid, where over-saturation and repetitiveness leads to waning interest, and thus the creators resort to cheap gimmicks like the “deaths” in Endgame, as well as drawn-out storylines geared towards hooking viewers on characters/series they haven’t been following, just so they can understand what the heck is going on. And just to agree with OP here: yes, the main plot of these two films really does seem incredibly dopey.

I get what you mean about the film being an ensemble with Thanos as the antagonist, but the thing is that Thanos is the only character in the movie that actually has any sort of story whatsoever, the only character that actually has some sort of drama based around him. He also is the character that has the most screen time, the character who drives what little plot the movie has, and the only character who impacts the ending of the movie. For all intents and purposes, he is the protagonist. If you view the film from the perspective that he is the antagonist, then the film is pretty much about nothing - basically just Thor getting a new weapon and then choking at the end when he tries to kill Thanos. 

I think the fan service of endgame is also definitely more so than the other ones, I mean the entire second act of the movie is literally them going back to old MCU movies and essentially showing a greatest hits compilation of popular scenes from previous movies in the series. And when I talk about the meta moments in the movie, I'm referring to stuff like "you're telling me you got your plan to save the world from watching Back to the Future"...

But ya I agree with pretty much everything else you said, and the comparison to Mad Mad World is an interesting one I hadn't thought of.

Man, that's pretty interesting. I was never into comics, so I don't know much about them, but it sounds like the movies really do mirror a lot of the same issues with the comics. Interestingly enough, I've also heard people talk about how the downfall of the comics in terms of the popularity foreshadowed what we're seeing happen with the MCU now, self imploding by releasing too much content, constantly raising the stakes, getting a bit too greedy, etc.

In addition to how he could just create more resources, another stupid aspect of Thanos' plan is how short-sighted it is. Using Earth as an example, if half the population suddenly evaporated, the world population would go back to 4 billion, which was the world population in 1975. So basically, all it would accomplish is setting things back 40 years before population growth brings us right back to 8 billion anyway. Obviously, there would be all sorts of chaos if the snap happened, who knows how it would impact population growth, but ultimately at most this would just buy us an extra 50 - 100 years before the overpopulation problem goes right back to where it started.
